title: Regulation of the polyamine pool in plants: Metabolic implications and stress mitigation, with emphasis on microbial influence

sections.abstract: Polyamines, found ubiquitously in all living organisms including plants, microbes, and animals, exhibit varied modes of action but share a common feature of directly or indirectly mitigating stress. This review seeks to consolidate pertinent insights into polyamine production in plants and plant-associated microbes, elucidating their influence on plant well-being. Among the major polyamines, including Spermidine (Spd), Spermine (Spm), and Putrescine (Put), their regulatory role extends to both biotic and abiotic stress responses, augmenting plant growth and development. Notably, Spd, for instance, has demonstrated efficacy in ameliorating physiological challenges arising from salinity, drought, heavy metal contamination, and heat stress. In addition to its abiotic stress alleviation functions, Spd contributes to biotic stress relief and tends to accumulate during pathogenic infections. Furthermore, Spd directly stimulates various aspects of plant growth by inducing molecular crosstalk with expansins, plant hormones, fatty acids, lipids, and amino acids, culminating in cellular enlargement. Plant growth-promoting microbes (PGPM), actively participate in polyamine metabolism. The exogenous application of polyamines leads to an augmentation of the endogenous polyamine pool, thereby positively impacting plant health, particularly under stressful conditions.
